layout_dets.text: ABSTRACT

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Potentiodynamic polarization experiments were performed in 0.1N hydro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chloric acid with 17% chromium ferritic stainless steels containing up to 3%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum and with 18% Cr-2% Mo ferritic stainless steels containing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 0-2% nickel and 0-2% titanium. Potentiodynamic polarization studies with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 17% chromium alloys were also performed in 1N hydrochloric acid and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in 1N sulfuric acid + 0.1N sodium chloride media. The critical current den-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sities were significantly decreased with an increased molybdenum content.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The pitting potentials were increased with increased molybdenum and ti-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tanium contents, whereas nickel additions had no effect. All materials were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensitive to crevice corrosion. Sulfate ions in the SO₄=: Cl- molar ratio of 5:1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inhibited pitting corrosion and suppressed crevice corrosion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effects of molybdenum on anodic polarization

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of 17% chromium stainless steels in sulfuric acid have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: previously been studied in this Laboratory (1). Be-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cause of the well-established usage of molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloying for increasing the resistance of stainless steel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to pitting corrosion, interest developed in extending

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anodic polarization studies to chloride media. It was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: envisioned that the anodic polarization in acidic chlo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ride media would not only provide information con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cerning the effect of molybdenum additions on the pit-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ting potential of ferritic stainless steels, but would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also provide some information concerning the active-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive transition of stainless steels in the presence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of chlorides.

layout_dets.text: Experimental Procedures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Two sets of laboratory-prepared ferritic alloys and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two commercial ferritic stainless steels (Types 430 and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4341) were investigated. The high-purity 17% chro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mium, 17% Cr-1% Mo, and 17% Cr-3% Mo laboratory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys were prepared by melting and casting in vac-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: uum. The resulting ingots were hot-rolled to 0.64-cm-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thick sheet, which was cold-rolled to a 0.32-cm thick-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ness, annealed for 1 hr at 815°C, and water-quenched.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys modified by titanium and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1 Type 434 is the proposed designation for stainless steel con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taining 17% chromium and 1% molybdenum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nickel additions were produced by induction melting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in an argon atmosphere, using the split-heat technique.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this technique, the base composition is melted, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of the melt is poured off to produce an ingot; then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the balance of the melt, the required alloying ad-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ditions are made and the next ingot is cast. This proc-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ess is repeated until a series of the desired composi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions is cast. The 18% Cr-2% Mo ingots were hot-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forged, hot-rolled to 0.76-cm-thick strips, and cold-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rolled to 0.38-cm-thick strips. The 18% Cr-2% Mo al-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: loys containing titanium were annealed for 1 hr at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1040°C, the minimum temperature that prevented for-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mation of a second phase in the high titanium alloy,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and then water-quenched. The rest of the 18% Cr-2%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mo materials and the hot-rolled, commercial Types 430

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 434 steels were annealed at 815°C for 1 hr and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: water-quenched. The chemical compositions of all the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: materials are given in Table I.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The electrodes for the potentiodynamic studies were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mounted in acrylic plastic, the exposed surface (0.5

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by 0.6 cm) always being a longitudinal section parallel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the rolled surface. A more detailed description of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the electrode can be found elsewhere (1). The exposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surface was polished using standard metallographic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: techniques, ending with a distilled water slurry of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 0.3μ alumina. For the pitting potential measurements,

layout_dets.text: the electrode surface was masked with electroplaters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experiments in 0.1N hydrochloric acid.—Typical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anodic polarization curves for the Types 430 and 434

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steels in 0.1N HCl are shown in Fig. 1. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active region for the Type 430 steel exhibited two cur-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rent maxima, one peak at —0.50v and another at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: —0.38v. Considerable variations in peak heights were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observed for different Type 430 samples, and in some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: samples the second peak was higher than the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peak. However, the corresponding potentials remained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approximately within ± 10 mv of the values given

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: above.² The single critical current density peak, shown

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the Type 434 steel, was always lower than the cor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: responding peak for the Type 430 steel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The passive region for the Types 430 and 434 stain-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noble than the normal transpassive transition range,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: +0.85 to +0.95v. This passivity breakdown for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unmasked electrodes was characterized by a gradual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increase in polarization current. A considerable amount

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: selected potentials without visible pitting or general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion. However, after a long potentiostatic polari-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: zation time, microscopic examinations revealed some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion at the boundary of the sample and at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: acrylic mount. This observation was in accord with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the results obtained by Schwenk (2). Thus, in all the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentiodynamic polarization experiments with un-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masked electrodes in HCl, the apparent passivity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breakdown was not due to pitting corrosion, but was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a result of the passivity breakdown inside the ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tremely fine crevice between the electrode and plastic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mount. The presence of crevices with the electrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mounted in metallographic materials was also indi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cated by Greene et al. (3).

layout_dets.text: Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pitting potentials in 0.1N hydrochloric acid.—The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: examination of the average pitting potentials for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 17% chromium alloys (Table IV) discloses that, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the molybdenum content is increased, pitting potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become more noble (i.e., the resistance toward pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion increases with the molybdenum content).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since a normal transpassive transition was obtained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the 17% Cr-3% Mo alloy, this material should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: immune to pitting corrosion under the experimental

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditions. However, Types 430 and 434, which are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commercial counterparts of the 17% chromium and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 17% Cr-1% Mo alloys, have significantly lower pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials. This difference in pitting potentials is prob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ably the result of the higher carbon levels and im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: purity contents of commercial steels, as compared

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the vacuum-melted laboratory alloys. Further-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more, the average pitting potential for the Type 434

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steel is only slightly higher than the pitting potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the Type 430 steel. The difference in pitting po-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tential was much more in the 17% chromium and 17%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cr-1% Mo alloys. Since the carbon level for the Type

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 434 sample used in this investigation was considerably

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher than that for the Type 430 sample [i.e., 0.069

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as compared with 0.046% (Table I)], it may be con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cluded that the higher carbon level obscured the effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of molybdenum on pitting potential. Higher carbon

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content in a ferritic matrix will result in more pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cipitated chromium and molybdenum carbides and in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a depletion of the matrix of chromium and molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum. Consequently, the ferritic steels with higher

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: carbon contents will probably have a greater sensi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tivity to pitting corrosion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The examination of the pitting potentials for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 18% Cr-2% Mo ferritic alloys, with a carbon content

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of about 0.03%, leads to the conclusion that small

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nickel additions (up to 1%) do not affect the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials of these alloys. In contrast to the insensi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tivity to small additions of nickel, small additions of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: titanium have a very pronounced effect on pitting po-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tentials. Titanium contents of 0.47 and 0.91% raised

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the pitting potential above the transpassive transition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A further increase in titanium to about 1.8% reduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting potential. Pitting potentials for titanium-modi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fied alloys, however, are still more noble than for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: titanium-free alloys. This effect of titanium could be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indirect. The titanium ties up carbon and nitrogen, pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: venting the formation of chromium and molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: carbides and nitrides and, consequently, prevents the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formation of zones depleted in chromium and molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum. With larger titanium additions, the consider-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: able amount of second phase that develops might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the preferred site for pitting attack.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mary passivation potential. In contrast to such pure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys as 17% chromium alloy, the commercial Type

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 430 did not show a critical behavior in 1N HCl, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Type 434 showed little tendency to passivate (Fig. 5).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This behavior is probably the result of the depletion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the ferritic matrix of chromium and molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the precipitation of carbides.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Smalì nickel additions to 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were somewhat beneficial to the attainment of passiv-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ity in 0.1N HCl, since these additions depressed the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: critical current density to the point where no active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: region was displayed. However, results from work on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: austenitic stainless steels (7) showed that an 18% Cr-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 16% Ni alloy free of molybdenum could not be com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pletely passivated in 1N HCl, but a similar alloy con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taining molybdenum could be. Thus, the beneficial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effects of small nickel additions to ferritic stainless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steel in HCl may be limited to the molybdenum-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing grades.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Polarization studies in HCl solutions revealed that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: HCl is an effective medium for the potentiodynamic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigation of the effects of alloying elements on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the corrosion and passivation properties of stainless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels. The effects of molybdenum additions are very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dramatically shown by polarization curves in 1N HCi;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is expected than any alloying addition which has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a strong effect on the passive film will also have a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronounced effect on the active-passive transition in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: HCl. Polarization curves in 0.1N HCl, especially with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 17% chromium alloy, were characterized by con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: siderable variations in critical current density and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: primary passivation potential. Such behavior would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probably result from the competition of the normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tendency of the alloy to passivate in a weakly acidic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: medium with the activating effect of the chloride

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: iops. Stainless steels with relatively weak passivation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tendencies would therefore be expected to have a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more prominently variable passivation behavior than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels with a strong passivation tendency. The active-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive transition region in 0.1N HCl was often com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plicated by the presence of two current density max-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ima. Since measured current is the difference between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the total oxidation and total reduction current, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small secondary current maxima might arise from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changing hydrogen evolution kinetics, which are the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: result of the passivation of the electrode surface. How-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ever, large secondary peaks observed with Type 430

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steel could not be explained. Since the potential for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either peak is fairly reproducible, the double-peak

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phenomenon for the Type 430 steel might result from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the chromium segregation and different passivation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behavior of chromium-rich and chromium-depleted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regions. For the Type 434 steel, which has a stronger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passivation tendency, the second peak is only slightly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicated (Fig. 1). Some support for the above specu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lation is given by the work of Voeltzel and Plateau

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (8) who observed a double-peak phenomenon for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensitized austenitic 18% Cr-8% Ni stainless steel. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double-peak phenomenon was ascribed to chromium

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: depletion along the grain boundaries.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: None of the ferritic stainless steels studied was im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mune to crevice corrosion in HCl, not even those which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: had a high resistance to pitting.

layout_dets.text: Polarization studies in sulfuric acid-sodium chloride

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution.—Since a complete passive range was obtained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for all the materials studied, the results from potentio-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dynamic polarization studies in 1N H2SO4 + 0.1N NaCl

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicate that sulfate ions in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ratio

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of 5:1 inhibit pitting corrosion. The inhibiting effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of sulfate ions on chloride pitting of austenitic steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has been described in the literature (5, 9). This in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vestigation showed that pitting corrosion of ferritic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steel can also be inhibited by sulfate ions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Furthermore, since crevice corrosion was very promi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nent in 0.1N HCl, it may be concluded that sulfate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions suppress the crevice corrosion to the extent that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a normal transpassive transition can be obtained with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a potential scanning rate of 0.540 v/hr.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Summary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Molybdenum additions to ferritic stainless steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: facilitated the attainment of passivity in 0.1 and 1N

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: HCl.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The pitting potential in 0.1N HCl became more noble

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with increased molybdenum content for high-purity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 17% chromium alloys and with increased titanium

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content for 18% Cr-2% Mo-0.03% C alloys. An in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crease in carbon content generally resulted in less

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noble pitting potentials, whereas small nickel addi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions (up to 1%) did not change the pitting potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significantly.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: All the ferritic stainless steels studied were very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensitive to crevice corrosion in HCl.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The sulfate ions, in a molar ratio of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5:1 not only inhibited pitting corrosion but also sup-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pressed crevice corrosion for all the steels investigated.
